# THE CALL of GOD
## And the
# REFUSAL of MEN.

In which one sees how God in these last times <note>Bourignon, like many mystics of her era, believed she was living in the "end times" or the final age of the world.</note> calls men, whether to the administration or to the participation of the fullness of his graces & of his divine banquet; what disposition he requires of them for this, and how they make themselves incapable of it by the refusal they make of it: and thus, *that many are called; but few are chosen*. <note>A reference to the Biblical parable of the wedding feast in Matthew 22:14.</note>

*The whole contained in this Collection of the first Letters of*
**Lady ANTOINETTE BOURIGNON,**
*(born in Lille, in Flanders, on January 13, 1616.)*

->to a person called by God, without having<-
->properly responded.<-

# TO THE READER.

We begin here, Dear Reader, to share with you one of the first works collected from among several left to us, after her death, by Mademoiselle <term>Antoinette Bourignon</term> <note>A controversial Flemish mystic (1616–1680) who claimed to receive direct revelations from God and gained a significant following across Europe.</note>. Her printed works, some of which have appeared in the past, will undoubtedly have already given you some knowledge of her person and of what you should expect from her. If, however, you have known nothing of her until now, this single piece is capable of forming in you a true idea of her character; especially since everything you will see here consists of <term>familiar letters</term> <note>The term "familiar letters" refers to private correspondence written in an informal, candid style, rather than formal documents intended for public debate.</note>, in which it is customary to reveal, with sincerity, the character of one's heart and one's spiritual state. These are letters written to a person from whom she neither should nor could hide anything, since she was writing them to a theologian who was her pastor and her confessor.

# TO THE READER

human instruction, yet full of divine and solid insights, providing instructions that are entirely heavenly and beneficial to her Pastor. One even sees in these writings precepts and an example of all the **Christian virtues**: of <term>mortification</term> <note>The spiritual practice of self-denial or physical discipline to overcome worldly desires.</note>, of holy retreat, of humility, of continual prayers, of attachment to God alone, of love for lowliness and afflictions, and of love for the salvation of one’s neighbor. 

But above all, one sees there the love of God in an admirable purity and activity; it is completely detached and selfless, burning and full of zeal, constant and undeterred from serving her God—whether facing persecutions from her own parents or the lack of response from men to the warnings she addresses to them on behalf of God. It does not matter, provided that this Love knows it has received from its God the commandment to *Call* people—whether many or few—to the banquet of God's graces; this is sufficient for her, without troubling herself about the rest. Their *Refusal* does not make her silent; their negligence does not make her slacken; their turning a deaf ear does not make her cease:

And indeed, one can observe from this point forward what this divine girl <note>original: "divine fille." This refers to Antoinette Bourignon, the author of the letters. Her editor uses this term to emphasize her spiritual purity and the belief that her insights were divinely inspired rather than learned from books.</note> clearly demonstrated throughout the rest of her writings and her life: that she sought only to call men solely to Jesus Christ, without attachment to herself, to anyone else, to a Sect, or to any party whatsoever, outside of the pure and unique love of God. ...responded to this call, that she herself fulfilled her duty in calling them. But alas! That is what she did not have the joy of seeing during her entire life. And it is not only the person to whom these letters are written who was found wanting in this duty, but even almost all the best among those who were most convinced of and held the greatest esteem for the divine truths she proclaimed. 

For as for the learned and the **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to high-ranking theologians and academic authorities of the Church.</note> of this world, they believed it would be to mock their Greatness and their Excellence to give the slightest place to the thought that God might call them through a woman. <note>original: "fille". While this can mean "girl" or "daughter," here it emphasizes her status as a woman without formal standing in the male-dominated Church hierarchy.</note> This thought is too base for their **Doctoral and Magisterial Highnesses**. <note>A sarcastic reference to the pride of university-trained theologians.</note> 

And as for the wicked and the passionate, they did to her the same things that all the **Messengers of God** have experienced, from the beginning of the world, from this perverse and wretched race. They persecuted her; they pursued her both within and outside her homeland; they defamed her; they seized her goods; they often poisoned her person; they even suborned murderers even within...

...her own house to massacre her; she did not find, in her last refuge, a place to rest her head with any security. But in this, God has done a double justice. He delivered this worthy soul from the miseries for which she sighed, to grant her the enjoyment of her Beloved; <note>In mystical literature, the "Beloved" refers to Jesus Christ, representing the soul's spiritual union with the divine after death.</note> and He has taken from men the presence of one of whom they were entirely unworthy, and whom the world did not deserve to possess any longer.

Nevertheless, all these things should not surprise us, nor leave us immeasurably astonished, since the Gospel predicts them to us clearly enough. # Table of the Letters contained in this Work.

Letter I. She exhorts them to detach themselves from worldly creatures, and to find solitude in God. <note>In this spiritual context, "creatures" refers to any created thing—people, possessions, or worldly desires—that might distract a soul from the Creator.</note>

II. She recounts how she entered into a life of penance.

III. A general desire for perfection is not enough; one must instead produce specific results.

IV. Why we are little moved by the Truth, and the remedies for this.

V. The futility of human conversations. <note>The author uses "conversations" here to mean social interactions and worldly talk that distract from spiritual contemplation.</note>

VI. Reasons for distancing oneself from the conversations of men.

VII. It is good to flee from people, but in moderation.

VIII. That the consideration of being a Child of God should lead one to despise all that is in the world, and to view it with indifference.

IX. From where come the zeal, the vocation, the self-offering, and the sorrow of A. B. for the salvation of souls. <note>The initials A. B. likely refer to Antoinette Bourignon (1616–1680), a controversial Flemish mystic who wrote these letters.</note>

X. How one must behave during temptations.

XI. How, in order to gain Heaven, the flesh must be submissive to the Spirit and be disciplined, with Divine help and joy. <note>The original French "être violentée" (to be violated/forced) refers to the biblical concept of "taking heaven by force" or practicing strict self-discipline over bodily desires.</note>

XII. Following the Call of God; and that one finds everything by leaving everything firmly and resolutely.

XIII. Constancy comes from God.

XIV. She responds to his question concerning what God demanded of him.

# And the Rejection of Men.
<meta>catchword: I</meta>

social interaction <note>original: *conversation*; in this context, it refers to social company and spending time in groups rather than just talking.</note> is harmful to the soul. This is why I tell you in particular, and with absolute certainty, that you will never arrive at true union with God so long as you love the company and friendship of creatures <note>original: *creatures*; meaning fellow human beings or created things as opposed to the Creator.</note>. I could well write an entire book of reasons to prove that human interaction is completely contrary to devotion; but for now, I only ask you to consider how few virtues you have acquired while in the company of others. Then you will say, along with me, that to give oneself to God, one must flee from men.

And even though you may have good reasons for going into company—such as to discover the impertinences and wickedness committed in the world, or to maintain order and provide a good example to prevent God from being offended—all these pretexts would be good if they were pure. But alongside these, there is a sensual inclination <term>portement sensuel: a worldly or physical drive or disposition, rather than a spiritual one</term> that excites a love for social company. Sometimes this is to favor someone, other times to seek recreation, or perhaps to receive honor or favor. To put it all in a word: if one always found as much good in the world as one desired, one would never want to leave it. But the world is in itself so wicked that it often wounds the one who wishes to caress it, and gives bitterness instead of sweetness to those who wish to taste it.

Yet one must not leave the world for that reason <note>i.e., merely because the world is unpleasant or bitter.</note>; but only to make yourself pleasing to God.

But when he conceals it, he commits the evil many times before God; and he curses in his heart the one who prevents him; and his anger lasts much longer.

This is why you must henceforth fight valiantly, without fearing the Devil—who has nothing but outbursts of fury—and have your total recourse to God, as I have said, who will never refuse you help in a situation that has no other goal but His glory.

### XVIII. LETTER.

->*Why we do not carry out our good resolutions. That we can do nothing without God.*<-

->MY FATHER,<-

We have nothing good within ourselves; yet God always generously bestows good things upon man; but He also necessarily requires that man acknowledge that he does not possess these things by his own means.

And to gain this knowledge <note>original: "connoissance." ### LETTER XIX.

#### On the sufferings and punishments after this life.

->MY FATHER,<-

You have great difficulty in firmly resolving to live virtuously; so much so that it seems to you to be a very painful thing to mortify yourself <term>mortify: the practice of self-denial or "killing off" worldly desires to strengthen the spirit</term> and to deprive yourself of what delights you. But this is for lack of knowledge, and because you do not consider the things that are to come. When you are dead, you will then see with what rigorous pain the negligence of this world must be paid for; but it will be too late. You will no longer be able to return.

# And the Refusal of Men.

I was once transported in spirit before Purgatory, where I saw the souls turning in the midst of burning flames, in the same way that one roasts meat to be eaten; but with this difference, that the meat is distant from the fire, and these souls are all in the middle of it, and the flame attaches itself to these bodies, as if one put a piece of wood in the middle of a great fire; so much so that the fat flowing from these bodies made the fire more ablaze, and caused them to roast, dry out, turn black and be entirely consumed; and nevertheless they remained always alive, giving such frightful cries, that the memory of it would still make my heart break <note>original: "fendre le cœur." A common idiom for heart-wrenching pity or sorrow.</note>.

->MY FATHER,<-

Consider all this very maturely. This is what you must set against those imaginary fears, by examining well whether it seems to you that the penance of this world is troublesome, or mortification painful, in comparison to that which must be suffered after death.

These are no fables. It will happen just so: And yet it will be the friends of God who will endure these torments for a time: for the wicked will endure them for all eternity.

I leave you now the choice of converting to God, or else waiting to make satisfaction in the future: For it is an infallible thing, that one must perform penance or else burn in the fire.

There is no other remedy. Your soul will never die, and it cannot hide itself from God. Whether you do good or evil, you must appear at the judgment of God.

But those who have acquired the Love of God <note>original: "l'Amour de Dieu." In this context, it refers to the theological virtue of Charity, or a total devotion to God.</note>, they will easily obtain humility and all the other virtues. So that for a conclusion I say, that one can indeed acquire humility without the Love of God; but not at all the love of God without humility, because God is too generous toward those who love him.

### XXV. LETTER.

*That one must not neglect the time of salvation.*

#### MY FATHER IN JESUS CHRIST,

IF you had two souls, I would pray to God that one might perish, so that you would know, at a dear cost, the importance of your salvation: for you do not know how to grasp it otherwise. I have such great pity to see you so lost, without my being able to find the means to bring you back to yourself. It seems to me in spirit that I see you in the agony of death, and that you look at me so sadly, saying, *Oh, why did I not follow you! Why did I not leave everything, to...*

### XXVIII. LETTER.

->*An example of how one must resolutely obey God, at the expense of everything.*<-

->**My Father in Jesus Christ,**<-

### LETTER XXX.

#### How one must serve God, without care for the rest.

->MY FATHER IN JESUS CHRIST,<-

I was quite astonished to hear that the Pastor of Blatton has been to Lille. I do not yet know what he will tell me. For the rest, I am joyful to hear that my father does not wish to listen to me <note>Bourignon often struggled with her father’s attempts to marry her off or control her inheritance; here she expresses relief that he is no longer interfering with her religious choices.</note>. That is all I expect from him: that he leaves me to serve God in peace. I ask for nothing else. And regarding what you say about providing me with a house, and also for the future, according to my devotion, I thank you most affectionately. I do not desire to be provided for, but rather to follow the <term>Evangelical Counsel</term> <note>These are the three "counsels of perfection" in Christian theology: chastity, poverty, and obedience. Bourignon is specifically invoking the vow of poverty and reliance on God's providence.</note> that one must not worry about tomorrow. Do not trouble yourself: God has provided until now, and He will provide for the rest. On this matter, I pray you follow the doctrine of Jesus Christ, to serve Him, and to have no care for the rest. Leave the dead to bury the dead <note>original: "Laissez les morts ensevelir les morts" — a reference to Matthew 8:22, emphasizing that spiritual duties take precedence over worldly or family obligations.</note>, and follow Jesus Christ perfectly, until God’s hour has come for us to see each other again, signing myself,

->Your daughter in Jesus Christ.<-

->*Antoinette Bourignon.*<-

From Mons, this 20th of November, 1639.

->*One must be inwardly firm in the ways of God.*<-

### LETTER XXXIII.

*On the same subject.*

#### MY FATHER IN JESUS CHRIST,

I am waiting for news from you to know what my father has answered you regarding the proposal in my last letter. I have heard that my sister came to find you on his behalf. I would very much like you to maintain a firm appearance toward her: For these people, who do not know virtue, mistake humility for confusion <note>original: *confusion*. In this context, Bourignon means that worldly people mistake spiritual humility for a lack of confidence or social embarrassment.</note>. I am sorry that you are taking so much trouble for me. I have much to do here to take God's side; because today it seems to the most learned minds that all perfection consists of human prudence <note>original: *prudence humaine*. ->*Antoinette Bourignon.*<-

# And the Refusal of Men.
### XLIX.

By the mercies <note>original: "par les entrailles," literally "by the bowels," a 17th-century idiom referring to the seat of deep compassion or the heart of Jesus Christ</note> of Jesus Christ, I beg you to give a little more hearing to the inspirations of God, and to do what you shall recognize through them. I seek the true path to Heaven. I ask your pardon for my freedom of speech: I have no desire to correct it.

I tell you nothing of my affairs, since you cannot assist me in anything. I have God: He is enough for me. I have heard that it is only the Jesuits <note>The Society of Jesus; Bourignon frequently clashed with established religious orders, who often viewed her independent mystical teachings with suspicion</note> of Namur who are tasked with withholding my letters; and that it is only those coming from Mons: therefore, one might still be able to give your letters to the Jesuits of Lille. *She earnestly exhorts him to surrender to the Call of God, particularly through the consideration of the things that God wishes either to declare or to work through her in these latter times.*

My very dear and very devout daughter in God,

->NICOLAS LAMBERT,<-
->Pastor of St. Maurice.<-

From Lille, this December 16, 1665.

### From another of his Letters.

->My dear and devout daughter in Our Lord,<-

I strongly desire to see one day the outcome of your affairs <note>original: "affaires" — Antoinette Bourignon frequently used this term to describe her divinely mandated mission to restore "true Christianity" on earth.</note>, in the hope of knowing the cause of the misfortunes that exist in the world, bringing about such disorders on all sides that even natural law <note>The "law of nature" (droit de nature) refers to a moral code believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, which Lambert argues is being ignored by society.</note> is no longer observed by men. People aim only to do their own will as they please, without caring if God is offended by what they intend to do. I wish to stop here on this point. You see and know more of it than I do. Would that it were my will that God would be so generous as to give me His light and His love together, so that I might follow the heavenly truth both in words and in works, just as He gives me the desire for it and leads me to prayer <note>original: "oraison" — specifically refers to contemplative or mental prayer, a central practice for 17th-century mystics.</note> to obtain it: for which purpose I implore your assistance and your entire mediation before God. Amen. .... I also expect in the future that God will fulfill in me what He has given you to see and know concerning me, and this through the hope that you will labor toward Him on my behalf for this purpose. Upon this, I declare myself to be what you know, and I remain forever,

->My dear and devout daughter in God.<-

->Your most affectionate in Jesus Christ.<-

->NICOLAS LAMBERT.<-

->Pastor of St. Maurice.<-

From Lille, this 18th of February, 1666.

# N O T I C E
### *regarding this Second Part*

## *The Call of God, etc.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral and foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

After what was said in the *first Part* of the Book bearing this title, there are only two or three words of advice to give, without otherwise detaining the Reader.

The first is that these Letters are collected from among many left by the late <note>The original French uses "feüe," a legal/formal term for the deceased.</note> *Mademoiselle Bourignon*; and those chosen to appear under this title treat roughly the same subjects as those in the *first Part of The Call of God*. They show that since man is detached from God (a detachment which is his misfortune) <note>original: "détachement qui est son mal"</note> and attached to a thousand other perishable objects—to sensory things, to pleasures, to money, to trade, to <term>offices<gloss>official positions or social duties</gloss></term>, to the world, to vice, to pride, to the vain speculations of the mind, to <term>self-will<gloss>the human ego's desire to act independently of divine guidance</gloss></term>, to one's own ways, choices, opinions, even ceremonies, and in a word to his own liking—God, condemning all these occupations that hinder man because He wishes to occupy everything within man Himself, calls him back from all that to Himself and to the spiritual and true means.

The letters have been arranged according to the order of their dates, as in the *First Part*, so that one may notice the constancy of the one who wrote them in serving God, in seeking only His glory, and in having throughout her life but one very pure and very holy design and goal: for the letters of the *First Part* begin from the 23rd or 24th year of her life: and in a continued sequence, the last ones in this volume were written two or three months before her death. One can also see through this progression of time how great is the hardening of men's hearts by how little fruit <note>The "fruit" refers to the spiritual results or conversions produced by her message.</note> it produced in them as she announced the will of God to them and redoubled her exhortations to follow it; and with how much reason she could say, as God does: *I have every day stretched out my arms to a rebellious people who speak against my words.* <note>original: "J'ay tous les jours tendu mes bras à un peuple rebelle & contrediſant à mes paroles." This is a reference to Isaiah 65:2, often cited in the New Testament to describe the rejection of a divine message.</note>

If some find that she was too difficult to please, and that she corrected too severely and with too much vigor even those who tried to obey God the most, noticing only the imperfections that might be in them without praising them or acknowledging the good that might also be there; I have only to tell them these words of the divine *Teresa* <note>St. Teresa of Avila (1515–1582), a Spanish mystic and reformer often cited by Bourignon’s editors to justify her rigorous spiritual standards.</note>, where, speaking of souls to whom God has given a care and love for the salvation of others, she says: (a) "Those souls can-

### I. Letter.

God Calls men out of their own spirit & their own will to submit themselves to His reprimands, to His wisdom, & to His divine will like little children: which, being unwilling to do, they do not profit themselves, and they harm a soul that enjoys communion with God <note>original: "l'entretient de Dieu," referring to an internal, prayerful conversation or state of being in God's presence</note> when they wish to converse with her. Neither God nor His own want anything that is not free. <note>Bourignon frequently emphasizes that spiritual devotion must be a result of free will, not forced by external pressure.</note>
->page 1<-

II. God Calls some out of the world by the hardships of wars; others out of their own will by the living declaration of His own: But the Devil & the corruption of nature cause them to oppose this divine Call, and strive to turn them away from it. Concerning which one must watch carefully.
->14<-

### LETTER I.

*God calls men out of their own spirit and their own will to submit themselves to His rebukes, to His wisdom, and to His divine will like little children: since they are unwilling to do this, they do not benefit themselves, and they hinder a soul that enjoys communion <note>original: "l'entretient," referring to an intimate spiritual conversation or dwelling with God</note> with God when they wish to converse with it. For the **Word of God** <term>Parole de Dieu: The divine logos or the direct speaking of God to the soul</term> is the nourishment of our souls, and He gives it to us fresh every day, just as He gave the **Manna from Heaven** <term>Manne du Ciel: The miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert, representing daily spiritual sustenance</term> to the children of **Israel** fresh every day. ## LETTER II.

*God calls some out of the World through the constraints of wars; others out of their own will by the living declaration of His own: But the Devil & the corruption of nature cause them to oppose this Divine Call, and try to turn them away from it. On which one must watch carefully.*

->My Child,<-

I have seen by your letter the arrival of the friends from **Friesland** <note>original: "Frise". A coastal region in the north of the Netherlands and Germany.</note>, whom I do not feel have come as purely for God as I desire; the wars have driven them away more than the love of the **Evangelical Life** <term>Evangelical Life (Vie Evangelique): A life lived in strict accordance with the teachings of the Gospels, often involving the renunciation of worldly wealth and status</term>. But I say to them as St. John did to the Pharisees, *Who advised you to avoid the evils to come? produce therefore fruits worthy of repentance.* <note>original: "Qui vous a conseillé d'eviter les maux à venir? faites donc fruits dignes de pénitence." I think that J. M. would have come to me even if there had been no war; but not his wife. As for R. J., he has often had the desire; but the Devil would have surely prevented him by one means or another; seeing that he still has great power over him.

# LETTER V.

->*To Major General van der Wyck, letting him know that the disgraces and adversities happening to him are a strong Call by which God wanted to draw him to Himself and disengage him from the world, which he is exhorted to no longer serve henceforth.*<-

Sir,

I think that all the tribulations and adversities that happen to you now are chains and bonds by which God wants to draw you to Himself, and that He allows all these things for your eternal good. He has spent a long time knocking at the door of your heart; but you have not opened to Him. All the interior lights <note>In Bourignon's theology, "interior lights" are moments of spiritual insight or divine inspiration granted directly to the soul.</note> that He has given you were not strong enough to make you leave the world, in which you were so engaged that a violence such as that which God uses now was necessary. Oh, for God’s sake!

act like salt waters, the more of which one drinks, the more one is parched: besides the fact that these natural pleasures or delights do nothing but rack <note>original: "boureller," meaning to torment or torture, as if by an executioner.</note> the soul after it has tasted them or sated itself upon them. ### LETTER VIII.

*Those whom God calls must be indifferent in following Him everywhere, without attachment to anything, but freely. The weak have need of the lights and guidance of others.*

SIR,

I received yours of the 8th of this month along with that of your wife <note>original: "Madame vôtre compagne." Bourignon frequently corresponded with couples or used "companion" to refer to a spouse in a spiritual context.</note>, who must be very dear to you, since she draws you to God. This is to be valued more than all the riches and pleasures of this life; for *what would it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses his soul?* <note>A translation of the biblical verse from Matthew 16:26, originally in French/Latin in the source.</note> I believe that God has bound you together, and that no one will be able to separate you. Many are bound in marriage by the instigation of the devil, or by the concupiscence <term>concupiscence: an intense longing or lust, often used in theology to describe the human inclination toward worldly or carnal desires rather than spiritual ones.</term> of their flesh: and those may well be divided by men; but this bond of charity <note>original: "charité," referring to divine, selfless love.</note> which is formed to help one another advance in solid virtue, through which one arrives at eternal life, is a bond from God: And even though you began through the flesh, you must finish through the spirit, so that your marriage may be blessed by God. And I believe that you may well follow your wife in this; for she seems to me more detached from the world than you are,

### LETTER X.

*One must avoid any appearance of a Sect, not teach before being perfect, but only bear simple witness to the truth when the occasion arises, without creating human structures. <note>The phrase "bâtiments d'hommes" (literally "human buildings") refers here to organized religious institutions or denominations, which Bourignon viewed as distractions from pure faith.</note> Those who are Called to be children of God will be cast out of the Kingdom of Heaven if they do not submit. Their refusal and resistance; which God does not wish to constrain, since he asks for everything through love and with freedom.*

My Child,

I DO not find it appropriate that you communicate the letters I write to you to others; seeing as that would take away my freedom to write necessary things concerning affairs or your private matters: And therefore do it no longer. But if there were something spiritual for the instruction or the nourishment of the souls of others in my said letters, you could extract it, or read only those things to them which would be useful to them, keeping the rest in secret for yourself.

God, just as the Children of Israel murmured against Moses: So that if they do not change, they must be cast out, & others will enter in their places. 9. I say all this as a final warning: for the Kingdom of Heaven is near; those who are not prepared will have no entry there. Each person must think of themselves, without regard for what others do; since it is written: *that of two being in one bed, one shall be taken & the other left.* <note>A reference to Luke 17:34, emphasizing that salvation is an individual matter and that close proximity to others will not save the unready.</note> We have had more than enough time to prepare ourselves well; but we have misused the opportunities that God gave in time. 10. I am no longer resolved to disobey God in this way for the sake of my Children. I prefer to stand alone to do in my private capacity what he commands me promptly, without being hindered by anyone. And my children will then do what they want, without my soul being soiled by their sins. For I have only promised to show them the will of God, insofar as they wish [to follow it].

### LETTER XIII.

*To Mr. Swammerdam <note>Jan Swammerdam (1637–1680) was a famous Dutch biologist and pioneer in microscopy who became a follower of Bourignon.</note>, advising him not to allow himself to be seduced by a call of self-love <term>self-love: original "amour propre," referring to vanity or ego-driven desire as opposed to divine love</term> to a Church of chimerical <note>Imaginary, deceptive, or impossible to achieve.</note> truth; and showing him divinely well how one must cooperate with the call and the graces of God, to attract continual ones, and arrive at the rebirth <term>rebirth: the spiritual "new birth" or total inner transformation central to Bourignon's theology</term>.*

It is a holy curiosity <note>Bourignon uses "bonne curiosité" (good/holy curiosity) to describe a healthy, spiritual desire to understand the state of one's own soul.</note>, very useful for the **salvation** of many, because people often perish on the path to **perfection** <term>perfection: In this context, the state of complete union with God’s will and the overcoming of the "ego."</term> for lack of discerning the state they are in; and they always want to judge the state of a soul in the same way; even though St. Paul says at one time of himself: *I do what I do not want to do, and I do not do what I want, finding in myself a contrary law:* <note>original: "Je fais ce que je ne veux faire, & ne fay point ce que je veus..." — A reference to Romans 7:15-23, describing the human struggle with sin.</note> And later when he finds himself in another state, the same Apostle says: *I no longer live; rather Jesus Christ lives in me.* <note>original: "Je ne vis plus, moy; ains Jesus Christ vit en moy." — A reference to Galatians 2:20.</note> These things are indeed contradictory, although both are very true without any contradiction. 

For when the Apostle speaks of the contradiction he felt in doing good, and that he did evil against his will, he speaks of the state in which he found himself when he fought the **corruption** of his nature, confessing that it induced him to do what he did not want to do, and prevented him from doing the good he wanted. But when this Apostle had overcome his corrupted nature, he no longer felt a contrary law within himself, and could say with truth: *I no longer live: but Jesus Christ lives in me.* Because the person who is **regenerated** in the Spirit of Jesus Christ no longer lives according to the movements of corrupted nature; but according to the movements of the **Holy Spirit**.

And such souls can no longer do anything to cooperate with the graces of God; because all their own functions cease, and they can no longer move of themselves.

6. I have found by experience that they were still attached to their own wills, not in everything submitted to the governance of God.

7. That is why it seems more expedient to me to treat the cooperation with the graces of God in the letter to W. B. * (which you have seen).

One must resist these two enemies and obey the ordinances of God. This is the only way of salvation, and I know of no other. If you know a better one, you may follow it. As for me, I prefer to walk alone on the path of salvation than to go in company on the way of perdition.

## LETTER XVI.

*While God suspends the retreat of his own <note>In Bourignon's theology, the "retreat" refers to her plan to lead her followers to a physical and spiritual refuge—specifically the island of Nordstrand—away from the corruption of the world and institutional churches.</note>, some advance by drawing closer to his children, and others slacken by distancing themselves and returning to the world; examples.*

I thought I would enter into my possession of Nordstrand <note>Nordstrand is an island off the coast of North Frisia. For I would rather never have this possession than to possess it through lawsuits and legal trickery. Our Brother Hening has been here for fifteen days, having absolutely abandoned the world. His wife thinks he has gone to seek service in the wars, as she had advised him. But he seeks to wage war against his vices and to win the victory over flesh and blood—over which he already has the advantage—and has obtained the gift of continence <note>original: "continence" — in this context, the spiritual grace of self-control and sexual restraint, which Bourignon viewed as essential for true devotion.</note>. He is so humble and fervent that he greatly edifies...

### & the Refusal of Men. Part II. Letter XIX.

->My good friend,<-

I see by your letter of the 12th of this month that you are resolved to abandon the world to serve God alongside us for the rest of your life. In this, you would be very happy. For there is nothing left to do in the world but to expect physical miseries and great perils for eternal salvation; seeing as we live in the <term>last times (the apocalyptic period preceding the end of the world)</term> predicted by Jesus Christ, which he compares to the time of Noah, saying that men *drank, ate, and married, without fearing the nearby shipwreck <note>original: "naufrage," used here as a metaphor for the Great Flood</note> that was to submerge them all.* It is exactly the same now: for one sees men eating, drinking, and marrying, without perceiving the plagues that God will unleash upon their criminal heads, nor the Reign of the <term>Antichrist (the spiritual force of deception that Bourignon believed had overtaken the world)</term> which now dominates almost all the minds of men. This makes their <term>conversations (social interactions and daily dealings)</term> very dangerous.

2. For what peril could be greater than to converse so familiarly with people who are bound to the Devil by a specific pact, who, under the appearance of virtue, try to win the affection of hearts; and when they cannot deliver them to the Devil through trickery and subtlety, they insult and persecute them? Such that the righteous person can no longer remain among them without suffering damage to body or soul. This is why a person is happy <note>In the sense of being "blessed" (French: "heureuse")</note> when they find the opportunity to be able to avoid the interaction of the world, which

### LETTER XXIV.

*The world draws those who remain in it into inconstancy and into sin. It is a great advantage to withdraw from it, and to live under the guidance and admonitions of an enlightened soul to embrace the Gospel life <term>vie Evangelique; a life modeled strictly on the teachings of the New Testament</term>. This must be done with freedom and through testing. Everything must be done openly and without regard for status among Christians. Christian Instructions;*

My Children,

I have received your letter in due time, in which you ask me for advice concerning your worldly possessions <term>biens temporels; material wealth or property, as opposed to spiritual "eternal" goods</term>. In this matter I could not precisely advise you, as I do not know the firmness of your resolutions. You tell me enough that you wish to let yourselves be governed by the will of God; but I have seen you change so often that I no longer dare to believe in your resolutions. I know well that it is God who gives them to you; but the Devil and the flesh <note>original: "la chair"; in this mystical context, it refers to human nature's inclinations toward sin and worldly comfort</note> often carry away this good seed. I truly believe that if you were out of the world, and conversing with us, you would be strengthened in virtue; since the Scripture <note>original: "l'Ecriture"; referring to Ecclesiastes 4:10</note> says, *Woe to him who is alone: if he falls, he has no one to lift him up.*

...anyone, saying only, *Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his Cross, and follow me* <note>original: "Celuy qui veut venir aprés moy, qu'il renonce à foy, prenne fa Croix, & me fuive"; a translation of the Latin Vulgate Matthew 16:24</note>, without saying, "You must do this or that"; but only, *if you wish*.

For it would be nothing but confusion if people were received into the company of Christians so lightly that they would change their minds again after having committed themselves. It would be better to test oneself for two years rather than one, or every day of one's life, rather than to repent of it afterward; since this repentance would cause trouble for you and for me, and **scandal** <note>In a religious context, "scandal" (scandale) refers to an action that might lead others into sin or cause them to lose their faith</note> to one's neighbor. This is why one must test oneself thoroughly before embarking on our community, where no one is sought after, but rather those who voluntarily join are assisted, as all true Christian brothers should do, among whom there should be nothing secret, nothing hidden or private; but all must be in common and sincere, without partiality or human considerations; and let him who has something bring what he has; and let him who has nothing be as well received as he who brings something, provided that he wishes to live as a true Christian.

6. I believe that you have not yet read enough of my writings to understand all my intentions in this regard, and that you do not yet know all that you would need to do and to **leave behind** <note>French: "faire & laisser"; a common spiritual phrasing in this era referring to active duties and the passive "leaving" or renouncing of worldly attachments</note> to live as a true Christian. This is why I intend to have the New Year’s letters printed under the title *The Renewal of the Evangelical Spirit* <note>original title: "Renouvellement de l’Esprit Evangelique"</note>, through which everyone will be able to see, without flattering themselves, whether they are a Christian or not, and whether they wish to submit themselves in all things to the **guidance of God** <term>gouverne de Dieu; in Bourignon’s theology, this is the total surrender of the human will to divine direction</term>, to be reborn in the **Spirit of Jesus Christ** <term>Esprit de Jesus Christ; the internal state of humility and love that replaces the selfish human ego</term>. This is something very few people know at present, because they have spoken of all these things as if they possessed them, though nothing could be further from the truth—even among those who aspire to **Christian perfection** <term>perfection Chrêtienne; the spiritual state of complete union with God's will, a major theme in 17th-century mysticism</term>, who in fact are Christians in name only, and are submitted only to their own wills, allowing themselves to be ruled by their sensual spirits instead of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. I shall clearly demonstrate this through this book, which a good friend is having printed for the benefit of souls of good will. It has grown considerably since its beginning was first seen. I hope it will benefit your souls and will show you more clearly than my own counsel what you ought to do and to leave behind. H. <note>likely a reference to one of her close associates or distributors, possibly related to her printing operations in Amsterdam</note> will ensure it reaches you in due time. In the meantime, make use of the letters I am writing to you, even though they contain **reproaches** <term>reprehensibles; here used in the sense of corrective rebukes intended to point out the recipient's faults</term>: they certainly spring from a holy affection, which seeks only the perfection of your souls. This you can be assured of by the one who takes very special care of them.

->This 8th of December, 1676.<-
->A. B.<-

<note>original vocabulary: Renewal of the Evangelical Spirit, Christian perfection, Spirit of Jesus Christ, guidance of God</note>

### LETTER XXV.

*One must not be discouraged by the weaknesses of others. Those who, after having begun to follow the Call of God, have returned to the world, have become much worse than they were before; for the world entangles one in all kinds of evils, and the Devil blinds them until he has placed them in a state where they can no longer escape his nets.*

Their inner selves must undoubtedly be tormented. I also pity poor J. He has presumed to have a conscience more just and true than the Holy Spirit. And when I tried to make him see this, he tried to blame me for the sins of which he was guilty, asking me for proof of my **justification** <term>justification; here meaning the defense or proof of one's righteousness and divine mandate</term> regarding things his conscience could not admit. To which I did not wish to respond, having done enough by showing him the truths that God teaches me. If he does not wish to receive or admit them, that is his concern; I must not justify the teachings of the Holy Spirit to erroneous consciences like his, which flatters itself only to lead to its own ruin. It is enough for me to have satisfied God by declaring to others what He teaches me, without wasting my time satisfying all the doubts or opinions of men, which would make me lose the time I employ in more useful and salutary things.

7. The New Year’s Letter has become a book titled, *The Renewal of the Evangelical Spirit* <note>original: "le Renouvellement de l'Esprit Evangelique"; published in 1669, this work outlined Bourignon's core philosophy of returning to the simplicity of the early Christian church</note>. You cannot have it so soon. It will be as useful as it is desired: for it teaches the children of God all that they must do and leave behind to be true Christians. You will be blessed if you follow it, letting others run to their perdition, since neither you nor I can help them when they voluntarily withdraw from the means of their **salvation** <term>salut; the deliverance from sin and its consequences, believed by Bourignon to be achieved through internal transformation</term>. God has planted me like a Tree on the earth, to bear salutary fruit and give it to others: But those who do not wish to taste this fruit may leave it for those who will taste it. If all the leaves of my tree have fallen in **Frisia** <note>a coastal region in the northern Netherlands and Germany where Bourignon lived and founded a community on the island of Nordstrand</note>, God pushes out new ones in **Germany** and toward **France**. I am relieved by the withdrawal of these Frisians; but it is up to them to work out their salvation as much far from me as near; since they are obliged to do what I have taught them to be saved, even if I were no longer in the world, or if they had never known me, nor heard speak of me. Therefore, never abandon them. The reading of these is the means by which God will illuminate you ever more. This I pray He may do, remaining forever,

Sir,
->Your most affectionate in<-
->Jesus Christ.<-

*This 2nd of March, 1677.*
->A. B.<- <note>A.B. stands for Antoinette Bourignon, the author of these letters and a controversial Flemish mystic who claimed to be a mouthpiece for God's direct revelations.</note>

### LETTER XXX.

*An exhortation to a person called by God, that by renouncing their own will, they should submit in simplicity to the will of God, which contains all perfection: against which the Devil tries to make those whom God calls oppose themselves, inspiring in them a spirit of contradiction in everything.*

->My Children,<-

I see that you still have great reluctance to do what I tell you, notwithstanding the strong resolution you made to obey me. This arises because you lose the memory that I am governed by the Holy Spirit. You believe this well in the depths of your soul; but when the occasion arises, having some matter to settle together, you take me for another person living according to the movements of their nature. And for this reason, you do not know how to obey me nor submit your judgment to what I say or do, even thinking sometimes that you would say or do better on your own than what I command. This comes from <term>Self-love: (French: *Amour propre*) In 17th-century spiritual contexts, this refers to the fallen human ego and pride that instinctively seeks its own path rather than God’s.</term>, which always esteems what it says or does more than what others might do or say. It is from this that quarrels and disputes arise, because everyone wants to be right and maintain their own opinion, or their own allegations. Schisms and ruptures in religion itself <note>Bourignon suggests that even the great divisions of the Christian Church are rooted in this same personal pride and refusal to submit to divine guidance.</note>

<vocab>Exhortation, will of God, Holy Spirit, Self-love, schisms, religion</vocab>

<summary>In this letter, Antoinette Bourignon rebukes her followers for their secret reluctance to obey her, attributing their resistance to "Self-love" rather than the Holy Spirit. She argues that true spiritual perfection requires the total abandonment of one's own judgment in favor of divine direction given through her.</summary>
<keywords>Antoinette Bourignon, obedience, Holy Spirit, Self-love, spiritual direction, ego, religious conflict</keywords>

### LETTER XLIII.

*When God reveals His light to those who are in darkness and in the life of the world, where one thinks only of working for <term>temporal<note>Meaning worldly or material concerns that are temporary, as opposed to eternal spiritual matters.</note></term> things, they must free themselves, renounce greed, and henceforth work only for God and to perform their penance, with as much or more ardor than they previously did for the perishable things of this world.*

If I had to move further away, I might perhaps come toward your area, where I would also need to remain unknown. This is why I thank you for the offer you made of your house: it is too frequented for me to remain there hidden and unknown. God will provide me with some place if I need to move away. This I shall wait to do with prudence. I conclude with my recommendations to you and to all your family, praying that God fills you all with His Holy Spirit. I remain

## LETTER XLIV.

*The <term>fragility<note>Bourignon uses "fragility" to describe the inherent weakness of human nature and its susceptibility to sin.</note></term> of our nature, the brevity of our life, the Call of God, the good opportunities He presents, the pains of sin, and the rewards of those who make the good choice, should lead us to leave <term>the world<note>In this context, "the world" refers to secular society and its distractions, which Bourignon viewed as the primary obstacle to a holy life.</note></term> and to follow Jesus Christ and His <term>lowliness<note>Refers to the "kenosis" or the voluntary humility and poverty of Christ.</note></term>, renouncing earthly pleasures in expectation of eternal ones.*

6. Nevertheless, the person must make the choice of these eternal pleasures and the renunciation of fleeting pleasures of their own <term>free will<note>The concept of "free will" (libre volonté) is central here; the author argues that while God desires our love, He will not force it, making our voluntary choice the defining factor of our salvation.</note></term>; since God never constrains anyone. He created man entirely free so as to be loved by him, which is the sole purpose of his creation. But when man turns his affections toward subjects other than God, He abandons and rejects him as a rebel against God’s designs; for God has no need of man, and lets him perish when he voluntarily withdraws his affections from God to place them in himself or in other creatures apart from God.

7. Regarding your proposal to come to me, I would wish it well if your heart were converted to God, and if you were willing to renounce yourself to embrace the <term>humility of Jesus Christ<note>The original French "bassesse" literally means "lowness" or "meanness." In this spiritual context, it refers to the voluntary adoption of a lowly social and spiritual status to imitate the poverty and suffering of Christ.</note></term> and become like a child to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. But if your heart is still worldly, seeking the delights of the world, you would not be very happy among us, who have voluntarily chosen a servant’s state, despising the world and its glory. If you knew how to resolve yourself to this humility of Jesus Christ, you would be happy to be with us, away from this perilous world; but if you lack this resolution, remain in the world. You will taste its bitterness along with its sweetness there, since these two things are inseparable. And if you had perfectly known its malice, you would leave it at this very moment, instead of waiting until <term>St. Remigius’s Day<note>St. Remigius’s Day (October 1st) was traditionally the date in France and the Low Countries when leases expired, debts were settled, and servants changed masters or renewed contracts.</note></term>, as you write in your letter; whereas the Scripture says: *Today, when you hear the* <note>original: "Aujourd'huy qu'entendez la [voix]" — A reference to Psalm 95:7 or Hebrews 3:7: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts."</note>

# The Calling of God,
<meta>catchword: Tra</meta>

*voice of the Lord, do not harden your heart:* <note>original: "voix du Seigneur, n'endurcissez point vôtre cœur." A reference to Psalm 95:8, often quoted in the New Testament to warn against delaying repentance.</note> For who knows if the Lord will knock for much longer at the door of your heart after it has received so many summonses without responding to them? In the 17th century, this was a common time for beginning or ending leases and changing residences.</note></term>, when you propose to come here. Here we have no permanent place, and I do not know where God will call me in the future: It is enough for me to remain faithful to him in every place, without choosing a fixed location for my own convenience, when Jesus Christ tells me *that he has no stone upon which to rest his head.* <note>original: "qu'il n'a pas une pierre pour reposer sa tête." Only this condition obliges us to change location, as we should willingly bear all other inconveniences as a <term>salutary penance<note>A "wholesome" or "health-giving" punishment. In this context, Bourignon views physical discomfort not as a misery, but as a spiritual medicine that helps the soul atone for past sins.</note></term>. I pray to God that he engraves upon your soul all the things that I write to you, so that you may put them into execution for the glory of God and for your salvation. This is what she wishes who loves your soul.

<header>Treatise on the Solitary Life</header>

# That the Solitary Life
### is the most perfect of all the
ways of life that exist in the world.
Written at the <term>Reclusage of St. André<note>The Reclusage of Saint-André in Lille was a religious site where individuals—often women—lived in total isolation or "reclusion" to devote themselves entirely to prayer and spiritual work.</note></term>, in Lille,
the year 1649. [the 33rd year of her age.] <note>The author, likely Antoinette Bourignon, frequently noted her age at the time of her writings to provide a chronological spiritual history.</note>

->I.<-
->*Advantages of the Solitary Life.*<-

O Solitary Life, how happy you are; and how pleasant, beautiful, and desirable you are to one who seeks God! You are more perfect than any other kind of life, of whatever dignity it may be.

It is in you that one hears the voice of God; not in the tumults of the affairs of the world.

It is in you that one acquires true spiritual light, which is darkened among the shadowy clouds of this age.

In you one discovers the state of one’s soul as if in a mirror.

In you one easily corrects all its defects, without being distracted by anyone, nor controlled, or hindered.

In you one enjoys a perfect rest and tranquility of spirit.

In you one feels the peace and joy of God with freedom. Finally, one dies to oneself, to be submerged and <term>dissolved<note>original: "liquifier." In mystical theology, this "liquefaction" or "melting" of the soul represents the stage where the individual's will softens and flows into perfect union with the Divine will.</note></term> in God.

<summary>This page serves as the introduction to a treatise on the spiritual benefits of seclusion, written in 1649. It extols the solitary life as the most perfect way to hear God's voice, achieve self-knowledge, and eventually find union with the Divine.</summary>
<keywords>Solitary Life, Reclusage of St. André, Lille, spiritual perfection, tranquility, mystical union, Antoinette Bourignon</keywords>

<page-num>214</page-num>
<header>On Life</header>

Oh, how happy is the soul that has chosen you for its mother; it shall enjoy the caresses of its <term>Beloved<note>In mystical writing, the "Beloved" almost always refers to Jesus Christ, following the tradition of the Song of Solomon.</note></term>, and shall find through perseverance its paradise on earth, in inexpressible delights.

I intend to examine all the states of the world, to see if my words are true, and if I shall conclude according to my proposition, *that the solitary life is the most perfect and happiest of all states of life that can ever be found in the world, for the body and for the soul.*

### II.

### *Advantage of the Solitary Life over the <term>Economic Life<note>original: "vie Oeconomique." In the 17th century, this term referred to the management of a household and family affairs, essentially the domestic life of a layperson.</note></term> and its inconveniences, both for the temporal and for the spiritual.*

Let us first take the state of *Marriage*, which is the most general. See for a moment to what servitude a person who marries is reduced! They make themselves a slave to the passions of another. They no longer belong to themselves, but to their partner: And in the difficulty of encountering two similar temperaments in two different people, they often fall into despair, seeing themselves preparing a matter of contradiction for every day of their lives.

How much trouble it is to mold oneself to the will of another, which will be entirely contrary to one's own! If you are chaste, your partner will be dissolute; if sober, they will be gluttonous; if miserly, they will be generous; and so with all the rest. When you wish to rest, yo<meta>catchword: u</meta>

And if it should happen (which is very rare) that you find a partner with some <term>harmony of temperament<note>original: "sympathie d'humeur." A matching of personalities or dispositions.</note></term>, do you believe you would be happy and content in your state of marriage? It is in vain to persuade yourself of that. For there are still a hundred thousand anxieties from which your state cannot be exempt. Firstly, if you choose a partner who is not of your age and status, there will be nothing but reproaches and taunts, as much from your partner as from their relatives. If you are less wealthy, you will be disdained; and if of lesser <term>birth<note>original: "extraction." One's social class or family origins.</note></term>, it will be held against you. If you are wealthier, your partner will lament, believing they endure many contradictions simply for not being as rich as you. If you have the satisfaction of having a partner who is beautiful and well-bred, they will be so proud of it that you will have great difficulty enduring them.

<header>On Life</header>

If God sends you no children, what torments and regrets! If you do have them, what anxieties in raising them! What care to make them wealthy! What hassles of <term>business dealings<note>original: "negoces." In this period, the term refers broadly to all worldly responsibilities, financial management, and social obligations required to maintain a household and its status.</note></term> and worries to provide well for them. The illness of one makes you die of grief; the death of another puts you in distress if they are well-bred and well-behaved. But if they lead a bad life, they will make you pull the hair from your head in displeasure. Having come of age, they will do everything contrary to the designs you have for them, and squander at will what you have earned with such labor.

This is the sum of the happiness of the state of Marriage; nothing remains but to leave your <term>partner<note>original: "partie." Used here in the sense of a legal or contractual party, referring to one's spouse.</note></term> to go give an account to God. What regret to have spent one’s life in so many pains, labors, toils, and sufferings, only to take nothing away, but rather to die in despair of abandoning what one has loved so much into the hands of children who will laugh at your struggles! Can one now call this state happy? Certainly, as far as *the body* is concerned, it is very miserable.

Let us see if it will not be the same as far as *the soul* is concerned. Alas! What means are there to achieve one’s salvation amidst so many troubles? One cannot see the state of one’s soul amidst so many entanglements. One cannot <term>devote oneself to God<note>original: "vaquer à Dieu." Literally "to be vacant for God," a spiritual term for clearing the mind of worldly noise to focus on prayer and contemplation.</note></term>, for the mind is always occupied with the business of the world. Night and day, one clings to one’s partner. What way is there to find the time or a heart free enough to attend to one’s soul? It is always the last to be served.

One falls easily into sins; but one rises up laboriously. If God comes to call this soul sometimes in the middle of its <term>worldly affairs<note>original: "négoces." This refers to the various social and financial occupations that distract a person from spiritual contemplation.</note></term>, it turns a deaf ear. If they make some resolution to withdraw for a short time to <term>attend to God<note>original: "vaquer à Dieu." This refers to one's partner in the legal and social contract of marriage.</note></term>, their children, or domestic affairs. Finally, it is very difficult to think seriously about one’s soul amidst so many difficulties in such a troubled life.

Let us then conclude with certainty, that this state is happy neither for the body nor for the soul, and that he who wishes to love God with all his heart, and to seek Him perfectly, has no business embarking on such a way of life. For he would be frustrated in his expectation. It is impossible for two opposites to remain together in the same subject. Peace is not found in trouble. Rest [is not found] in anxiety, nor the love of God in carnal love. These are subjects too contrary. It is folly to hope for them.

Oh, how happy the **Solitary Life** is compared to this life and state of **Marriage**! It is my view that the one is a Paradise and the other a <term>temporal Hell<note>The author uses "temporal" to mean a hell experienced during one's time on earth, rather than the eternal afterlife.</note></term>: insomuch as in hell, there are only pains, darkness, troubles, and confusion, and finally despair. In Marriage, it is just the same. It is nothing but bodily pains and infirmities, darkness of spirit, and continual troubles and annoyances, with the confusion of various accidents of

<header>Solitary</header>

What pleasure is there in well-seasoning one's belly and seeking out delicacies <term>friandises: refers to sweet or gourmet treats, often associated with the sin of gluttony</term>? He who habituates himself to his tongue <note>meaning someone governed by the sense of taste</note> is never satisfied in his appetites. He always covets what he lacks. Too much food makes the body and the spirit heavy and sluggish. The seam of a shirt of fine linen will cause it pain. Finally, it will not be able to move itself without hurting itself.

And that on the contrary, the way of life of even the least perfect solitaries is happier regarding the body, and more perfect regarding the soul, than the way of life of the worldly; as it is more quiet, less laborious, and more exempt from opportunities to offend God.

### IV.

*That the solitary and retired life is preferable to the free life of people who occupy themselves with performing good works for their neighbors, because of human fragility: but not otherwise.*

But a doubt remains in my mind, namely: if a person remaining free in the world were to occupy themselves with performing good works of charity and piety, and set out to draw and convert the world to God; would they not be happier in body and soul than a solitary, who seems to do good only for themselves?

To express my view on this, I believe that if it were possible for a person living in the world to be perfectly dead to themselves <note>original: "morte à elle-même"; a common ascetic concept referring to the total renunciation of one's ego, pride, and personal desires to become a vessel for divine will</note> and to all the feelings of nature; and that amidst all the worldly storms and perils they remained firm and unshakable in continual union with God; that would seem more perfect to me than solitude. This is because, beyond the perfection of their own soul, they could cooperate <note>In this theological context, "cooperate" means to work in harmony with God's grace to achieve the salvation of others</note> in the good of others without harming themselves.

But as this is difficult considering our human fragility, it seems to me altogether impossible according to the experience I have of it. How many times have I faltered in my good resolution? In how many perils have I found myself among...

With what happiness, then, could one be filled who strives to convert the world—whether for the body or the soul, through preaching or private meetings—compared to a solitary <note>original: "solitaire"; a person, such as a hermit, who lives in religious isolation to focus on prayer</note> who strives to unite with God, withdrawn from the world? He who makes a profession of teaching the world through *Preaching* or otherwise is always in the labor of coming and going, of studying, and of ruminating deeply on what he will do or say to others. His body and his mind are in constant agitation; even the nights grant him no rest. And when he has labored the most, he will know the least what to do. If he thinks to please one person, he will displease a hundred.

All the care he takes to fulfill his duty often gnaws at his heart. He racks his brain with study, wears out his throat with shouting <note>The original "se créve l'estomac de crier" refers to the extreme physical strain placed on the lungs and stomach during long, loud sermons delivered without modern amplification</note>, and exhausts his body with travel. And when he has done all this, he depletes himself and leaves others to die of hunger.

And for the Soul, there is no less advantage: for he who occupies himself with others usually has nothing but a forgetfulness of himself and of his own perfection. Since the state he is in obliges him to occupy himself more with the exterior for others than with the interior for himself, the others gain no profit from it, and he himself gains even less. Everything flies away in the wind—both the labors of the body and the perfection of the soul.

The voice is only for the sake of others, and is useless to ourselves; for we know well enough what we are thinking without needing our voice to express it to ourselves. Similarly, everything we teach to others is of no use to us if we do not practice what we teach. It is nothing but pure vanity before God, and there is great danger that vainglory <term>vainglory: the pursuit of empty praise or taking pride in one's own religious accomplishments</term> may creep into our souls through these exercises, insensibly and without our noticing.

You receive within your Soul as many lessons as you must practice, remaining free from all curiosity <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "curiosity" often referred to a restless or vain desire for worldly knowledge that distracted from God.</note>, and no longer seeking the superfluous sciences you might have acquired in sermons! He who speaks to you in the depths of your soul is true Wisdom <note>original: "sapience"</note>. You alone hear Him, to the exclusion of all those who are occupied with the cares and clutter of the earth. Live happily in your retreat, drinking deeply from the Fountain of Life, while others languish in thirst among the cracked cisterns <note>A biblical allusion to Jeremiah 2:13: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."</note> of human sciences.

If *Confessions* are more frequent in Cloisters than in solitude, it is because those in cloisters have a greater need for them, being more prone to sinning among men than when they are removed from them. How many causes for grumbling among a community! How much envy slips into hearts, and wrath, and little barbs <note>original: "broquarts"; sharp, mocking, or sarcastic remarks</note> one gives to another, mockery and contempt for one’s neighbor, slander, impatience, condemnation, pride, partiality, lack of charity, grumbling, discontent, curiosities, covetousness, avarice, lies, insolent laughter, sadness, disorder, sorrow, arrogance, idle words, useless actions, flattery, and a thousand other imperfections are by no means banished from the Cloisters.

For against whom could he be angry, grumble, and murmur? He who is always alone, what can he covet, seeing nothing? If the Solitary is deprived of *Frequent Confessions*, it is because they are not necessary to him. And if sometimes he has need of them, he can have them. O Solitary, how happy you are to be away from so many opportunities to offend God, and from so many perils of having to return to grace; even if there were only this single good: to see oneself away from so many opportunities and perils of sinning. # Of Life

For it is impossible to be **recollected** <note>In a spiritual context, "recollection" refers to a state of inner stillness and focusing one's mind and heart entirely on God.</note> amidst so many distracting objects. It would be much better to receive **Communion** <note>The sacrament of the Eucharist, or the Lord’s Supper.</note> only once a year with the proper disposition, than to receive it three hundred and fifty times out of custom and without preparation—as do most of those who receive it daily. This is made manifest enough by the lack of effect and growth in **virtues** seen in those who are daily nourished by this **heavenly food**. <note>A traditional metaphor for the bread of the Eucharist.</note> One often sees them as imperfect after fifty years of **religious profession** <note>The formal commitment to a religious order through the taking of vows.</note> and many thousands of Communions as on the first day they entered the **religious life**; indeed, one even sees them diminish in their love of God.

For it is certain that no one reaches the profession of religion without having received a particular **grace** from God. However, the multitude of external things practiced there obscures the inner light that God had given to the soul; this causes all religious functions to be performed by habit, without feeling and without spiritual profit. This is why one encounters so few perfect and truly **spiritual** religious people.

If one received Communion worthily even once in their life, God would enter the soul as if into His own dwelling, and He would work all the virtues necessary for the preservation of His **union**. <note>The mystical union between the human soul and the Divine.</note> One would see this heart detached from all earthly things, a contentment in the soul, a joy in the spirit, peace amidst trouble, continual rest, and finally a wit-

# On Life

Do not say also that the **Solitary** <note>A hermit or recluse living in devotion.</note> is deprived of the merit of *Obedience*; for he obeys God more perfectly than any others, following in everything His holy commandments and, besides this, the **Evangelical counsels** <note>The "Evangelical counsels" are the three virtues of poverty, chastity, and obedience, traditionally based on the teachings of Jesus in the Gospels as a path to perfection.</note> to the letter. This is no longer observed in **Religion** <note>In this context, "Religion" refers specifically to organized monastic life or religious orders (e.g., being a "Religious").</note> any more than elsewhere.

For what religion is there today that actually renounces the comforts and possession of temporal goods? If they leave some goods behind to enter religion, they seek them with more greed and affection once they are in it than even worldly people often do. And they have many reasons for doing so. But I fear greatly that these [reasons] will not be accepted before God.

The most perfect obedience is [to obey] God. And why are they more exact in obeying their **Superiors** <note>The head of a religious house or order.</note> than God Himself? A Superior will command one to take good care for the morrow, so that nothing is lacking in the house; and God forbids taking care for it. <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 6:34: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow."</note> But no one listens to Him. One relies more on temporal goods than on His word. God says that one must be *poor in spirit*; and a Superior will despise you if you are not eager to profit the house. In short, the commandments of men are much more [obeyed] than those of God.

It is quite true that for persons who are accustomed to evil, they do well to put themselves under the **discipline** <note>A system of rules and training for conduct.</note> of a Superior, in order to break and correct their imperfections by force of obedience: but a Solitary, who renders internally to God...

I speak only of *those who in heart, affection, and will, live in the forgetting of all created things, to be united to God alone.* These are the most perfect people in the world. For there is nothing that can surpass union with God, which Solitaries alone enjoy. For what means is there to find Him in the company of men? Everything that one sees, hears, and says is but a distraction <note>Original: "detourbier," an archaic term meaning a hindrance, disturbance, or something that turns one away from a path.</note> from this union.

Should the Solitary fear this? If he has had the strength to leave the whole world behind and withdraw into seclusion, he has already conquered all his fears. He laughs at these *terrors*; because he has placed his trust in God, who makes him unshakable.

And as for *vainglory*, he <note>The Devil.</note> will gain nothing there: because the more a soul approaches God, the more she knows herself. Her nothingness is so evident to her, and the mercy of God toward her so well known, that she could never attribute anything to herself but sin. Therefore, he will lose his labor.

And if he tempts him with *lust*, what disposition will he find in him to make him fall? A body weakened by penance and austerity. And if he finds it difficult to remain chaste, what difficulty would a Religious <term>Religious: A person living under monastic vows, such as a monk or nun.</term> or a Secular <term>Secular: A person living in the "world" (the *siècle*), including laypeople or clergy who are not members of a monastic order.</term> have, who indulges the body in comforts, without fearing temptations...

### On Life

...temptations of the Devil; who has many more means at hand to tempt a Religious <term>Religious: In this context, a "Religious" refers to someone living under monastic vows in a community (like a monk or nun), as opposed to a "Solitary" or hermit.</term> or a worldly person, than he does a Solitary.

Because all creatures <note>In 17th-century spiritual French, "creatures" refers to anything created by God, including people, animals, and physical objects.</note> cooperate in his designs, money serves him as a means to tempt with greed; women, with lust; men, with anger; meats with gluttony; the virtuous, with envy; the lukewarm, with sloth; wine, with drunkenness; discussions, with lies; and conversations, with slander. And so it goes with all others. What the Devil cannot do himself, he stirs up creatures to do for him.

See then if a Religious is not subject to far more temptations from the Devil than the Solitary; the latter can never suffer more than two or three, and with this, he is fortified by God. For the further one moves away from men, the closer one is to God. Less human help means more union with God.

All the creatures of the earth act as so many stumbling blocks to virtue. All men are covered in pitch: one cannot touch them without being stained by their filth. You may well suspect that the Devil will win many souls throughout the world, seeing as he has so many nets <note>Original: "rets," meaning snares or fishing nets used as a metaphor for spiritual traps.</note> to catch them without their noticing. But as for the Solitaries, they are in safety, in the harbor of salvation, where the Devil has no entry.

# Confession of Faith of Mademoiselle Bourignon, which she presented to the Court of Gottorf <note>The Schloss Gottorf in Schleswig, where Bourignon sought refuge in 1671 under the protection of Duke Christian Albrecht.</note>, to oppose the slanderous rumors that the Clergy were spreading to make the purity of her Faith suspect.

->I.<-

I am a Christian, and I believe everything that a true Christian must believe.

->II.<-

I am baptized in the Catholic Church in the Name of the Father, in the Name of the Son, and in the Name of the Holy Spirit.

->III.<-

I believe the twelve Articles of the *creed* <note>original: "credo"</note>, or the Apostles' Creed <note>The Apostles' Creed is a foundational statement of Christian belief used by many denominations to summarize essential doctrines.</note>, and do not doubt any article thereof.

->IV.<-

I believe that **Jesus Christ** is True God, and that he is also True Man, and that he is the Savior and Redeemer of the World.

->V.<-

I believe in the Gospel, in the Holy Prophets, and in all the Holy Scripture, both the Old and the New Testament.

## MERCY
### OF GOD.

Which discovers all essential Truths regarding the Matters of the True Christian Faith; even those which have not yet been heard nor understood by men, nor even revealed by God, who has reserved them for the last times, in which we now live, where all things shall have their fulfillment in a perfect and accomplished sense. <note>Bourignon’s writing often reflects the "millenarian" belief that she was living in the final days of the world and was tasked with revealing divine secrets previously hidden from humanity.</note>

->Composed by<-
### ANTOINETTE BOURIGNON.
### FIRST PART.

->THE COAT OF ARMS<-

<image-desc>A heraldic shield featuring a large fleur-de-lis. The shield is surrounded by text on all four sides, forming a square border around the central emblem.</image-desc>

<margin>OF THE LILY IN FLANDERS.</margin> <note>original: "De la Lis en Flandres." The fleur-de-lis is the traditional heraldic symbol of the city of Lille.</note>
<margin>OF THE CITY OF LILLE</margin> <note>original: "De la Ville de l'Isle." Bourignon was born in Lille (historically "L'Isle" or "Rijsel").</note>
<insert>UPON THE RIVER</insert>
<note>The text "UPON THE RIVER" is printed upside down at the bottom of the heraldic emblem, likely referring to the Deûle river which flows through Lille.</note>

->IN AMSTERDAM, at the house of *Jean Rieverst* & *Pierre Arents*,<-
->Booksellers, Exchange Street, 1681.<- <note>Amsterdam was a center for radical religious publishing in the 17th century, providing a safe haven for authors like Bourignon whose works were often suppressed elsewhere.</note>

<meta>Handwritten initials "S.K." at the bottom of the page.</meta>
